triage.reason: SUP-07's exculpation is that the package is a recognised official fork or port with a long history and a matching maintainer, or that the similar name predates the popular one. Settling that requires the four registry signals SUP-07's minimal test names, and this engagement is offline with no registry query permitted, so none of the four -- existence, first-publication date, download volume, maintainer-versus-repository -- could be obtained. The condition could not be established in either direction, which caps this finding at `probable` and forbids `confirmed`.

Invoked additionally, because absence of an import is the tempting way to dismiss this. It does not apply: the entry sits in `dependencies`, not `devDependencies`, so the package is fetched and its install hooks run on every consumer install regardless of whether any code imports it. The shipped-path question is settled by the manifest, not by the call graph.

findings.inference: That `lodahs` is not a legitimate package is inferred, not observed. What was observed is the name's single-character distance from `lodash`, its placement in production dependencies, and that nothing in the tree imports it. The registry evidence that would confirm or refute it -- SUP-07's four signals -- was unobtainable offline, and the package body was never present to read.
findings.limits: Says nothing about what the published `lodahs@1.0.1` contains: no dependency code was available and none was fetched. It also does not assert the reverse -- a package with a confusable name can be benign, and the recommendation is written so the read-only registry check settles it before anyone treats machines as compromised.

findings.title: Non-text artifact tracked and published under vendor/ with no build recipe and no reader
findings.evidence: `file vendor/billing-native` reports `ELF 64-bit LSB *unknown arch 0x7574* (SYSV)`; the first eight bytes are a genuine ELF ident (7f 45 4c 46 02 01 01 00), so this is a non-text tracked artifact rather than a misclassified text file. Its provenance is disclaimed by the repository itself at vendor/README.md:1-2: "`billing-native` is a fixture standing in for a compiled helper. It is not the output of any recipe in this repository." A search of every file in scope for a reader (`grep -rn 'billing-native|vendor/'`) returns only that README and the two constants in scripts/fetch-native.js:17-18, which name a same-named artifact fetched from the network to /usr/local/bin -- a different file, not this one. No build step, script or shipped file reads vendor/billing-native. With no "files" allowlist in package.json and no .npmignore, it is nevertheless packed into the published tarball.
findings.impact: The package distributes an opaque, non-reviewable artifact whose origin the repository explicitly cannot account for, and which no scanner in this discipline can see -- osv-scanner, trivy and grype are structurally blind to a blob with no manifest entry and no version, so a clean run over this repository would prove nothing about it. Today it is dead weight in the tarball rather than an execution path; the risk it carries is that a future build step or entry point can start reading it without anyone re-deriving where it came from, which is precisely the half of CVE-2024-3094 that lived inside the repository rather than in the release.
findings.preconditions: For any execution impact, a build step or shipped code would have to read or execute the file. None does in the tree as read.
findings.recommendation: Either delete it, or make it accountable: commit the recipe that produces it in this repository so it can be regenerated and diffed, or replace it with an upstream artifact pinned by digest whose source you can compare. Whichever way, add a `"files"` allowlist to package.json so unaccounted files cannot ride along into the tarball, and add a check that fails the build when a tracked non-text file has no documented origin (`git ls-files -z | xargs -0 file --mime-encoding | grep -w binary`, minus a declared allowlist).

triage.reason: SUP-23's exculpation is that the binary is the declared output of a recipe living in the same repository and can be regenerated, or is a vendored artifact pinned by digest whose upstream source can be diffed. The repository rules this out in its own words at vendor/README.md:1-2 -- it is not the output of any recipe here -- and no digest, version or upstream reference for it appears anywhere in scope.

SUP-23's classifier caveat is that an unusual encoding or one enormous minified line made `file` call a text file binary. That is not the case: the file opens with the ELF magic number and NUL bytes and is classified as ELF, not as text with odd encoding. The second exculpation -- inert data such as an image, font or golden file -- was tested the way SUP-23 requires, by looking for the reader rather than by the file's location, and no reader exists; but 'nobody reads it' makes it dead weight, not accounted-for data, which is why this is reported as hardening rather than dropped.

findings.limits: The blob is 42 bytes and carries an unknown machine architecture, so it cannot be a functioning executable as it stands; this is reported as a provenance and packaging defect, not as a live payload, and the evidence states the size rather than implying more. The search for a reader covered only the 9 files in scope: the entry point declared at package.json:6 (bin/billing.js) is absent from the tree, so a reader could exist in code this audit never saw -- that is the one path by which this would stop being hardening.

findings.title: Published artifact carries no provenance attestation and no signature
findings.evidence: package.json:10 `"release": "npm publish"` -- a bare publish with no `--provenance` flag. `grep -rn 'cosign|slsa-verifier|gh attestation|gpg --verify|sha256sum'` over the whole scope returns nothing, so no signing or verification step exists anywhere in the tree, and there is no .github/ or other CI configuration that could attach an attestation. package.json:4 `"private": false` confirms the package is meant for a public registry. The result is SLSA Build L0 for an artifact that, per F-001 and F-002, runs code on its consumers at install time.
findings.impact: A consumer has no way to bind the tarball they install to a source commit, a builder or an identity: nothing distinguishes a release built from this repository from one produced by whoever holds the publishing credential. This grants an attacker nothing on its own -- it removes a detection and attribution control rather than opening a path -- which is why it is recorded at informational. It matters more than usual here only because the package executes an install hook, so the artifact consumers cannot verify is also the artifact that runs.
findings.preconditions: Becomes load-bearing only if the publishing credential or the maintainer account is compromised; SUP-10 is the procedure for that question, and it could not be exercised (see ruled_out).
findings.recommendation: Publish from CI with npm's OIDC Trusted Publishing (`permissions: id-token: write`) and `npm publish --provenance`, so each release carries a signed attestation naming the commit and the builder; npm classic tokens were revoked on 9 December 2025 and granular write tokens are capped at 90 days, so a stored NPM_TOKEN is no longer the right shape regardless. Then state the SLSA Build level the project targets and check releases against it, rather than treating provenance as optional documentation.

triage.reason: SUP-12's exculpation is that the registry already stores provenance attestations from a hosted builder which the consumer verifies. There is no hosted build path in scope at all -- `release` is a bare `npm publish` run from wherever the maintainer stands -- so no unskippable layer produces an attestation.

SUP-12's other exculpation is an artifact consumed only internally, by immutable digest, from an access-controlled registry. package.json:4 sets `"private": false` and .npmrc:1 points the unscoped default registry at registry.npmjs.org, so the consumer is a second principal outside the publisher's perimeter.

Real but bounded to informational. No exploit path is asserted: the absent attestation is a defence-in-depth and attribution control, and its absence gives an attacker no capability they did not already have. Recorded rather than deleted, exactly as FP-10 requires, because it is the control that would have contained F-001 and F-002 had the publishing account been misused.

findings.limits: Established from the tree only. Whether the npm registry already holds attestations for previously published versions of @acme/billing-cli was not checked -- that requires a registry query, which this engagement did not perform -- so this describes the release path as configured here, not the history of the published package.

findings.title: Lethal trifecta in one support agent: customer-written text, billing data and credentials, and an unrestricted outbound and execution channel
findings.evidence: Per-agent capability inventory built from the files in scope, one row per capability. (1) Private data and credentials: agent/answer.py:59-64 `issue_refund`/`lookup` operate on billing accounts; agent/answer.py:7 reads ANTHROPIC_API_KEY from the process environment; config/mcp.json:3-7 places a literal billing API key in the `billing` server's env, in the same deployment. (2) Untrusted ingestion: agent/memory.py:26-28 `ingest_ticket` indexes `ticket["body"]`, text written by whoever files a support ticket, and agent/answer.py:11-13 `build_prompt` concatenates retrieved documents into the same flat string as SYSTEM. (3) Outbound and execution channel: agent/answer.py:48 `subprocess.run(model_output, shell=True, ...)` reaches the whole shell grammar and therefore the network and every credential the process user holds; agent/answer.py:30 `issue_refund(decision["account_id"], decision["amount"])` is a state-changing effect whose destination the model names. Three marks on one agent.
findings.impact: An attacker who files a support ticket writes text that the agent reads with the standing of an instruction, and that agent holds both the billing credentials and a shell. The attacker does not need a flaw in any component: the composition is the flaw. The reachable outcomes are refunds to an attacker-chosen account, disclosure of another account's data through `lookup`, and arbitrary command execution on the host with ANTHROPIC_API_KEY and the billing key in the environment.
findings.preconditions: The attacker can put text into the retrieval corpus, which for a support product means filing a ticket. No account on the target system and no authentication beyond that is required.
findings.recommendation: Break a leg; do not add a sentence to SYSTEM asking the model to ignore instructions in data, which is a request rather than a control. In order of effect: (a) delete `summarize_and_run` and remove the shell entirely, since nothing in a support assistant needs it; (b) route every tool through `run_tool_scoped`'s shape, so the authenticated subject and not the model names the object, and keep refunds outside the assistant's reach; (c) isolate ingestion behind the Dual LLM or Plan-Then-Execute pattern, where the component that reads ticket text holds no credentials and returns typed values to a privileged orchestrator, or enforce capabilities at the call site as CaMeL (arXiv:2503.18813) does.

triage.reason: No layer sits between ingestion and the sensitive capabilities that a call must pass through. The four safer variants in the tree (build_prompt_marked at answer.py:16, run_tool_scoped at answer.py:36, summarize_and_render at answer.py:51, ingest_ticket_marked at memory.py:31) are sibling functions a caller may simply not choose, and triage.md FP-01 states explicitly that a control a caller may forget is not this rule.

A second principal is named: the ticket author at memory.py:28 is not the account holder whose records `lookup` returns and whose money `issue_refund` moves at answer.py:59-64. The two identities are distinct and the boundary between them is crossed inside one agent.

findings.inference: That one agent holds all three legs at the same time. The three capabilities are located in one module set, one process environment and one MCP configuration, but agent/answer.py:7 builds an Anthropic client that is never called, so there is no agent loop in scope proving the legs are composed in a single session rather than belonging to separate entry points.
findings.limits: Establishes the composition from the code that is present. It does not establish that the deployment wires the unsafe variants rather than the safe ones, and it does not enumerate egress channels outside these files: no renderer, HTTP layer or CSP is in scope, so a markdown-image channel (AI-16) would be an additional leg neither confirmed nor excluded here.

findings.title: Model output executed as a shell command with shell=True
findings.evidence:
agent/answer.py:46-48

    def summarize_and_run(model_output: str) -> str:
        """Runs the shell snippet the model produced for the operator."""
        return subprocess.run(model_output, shell=True, capture_output=True, text=True).stdout

The function's only parameter is the model's text, the docstring names it as such, and it reaches `subprocess.run` with `shell=True` without validation, quoting, allowlist or sandbox. Source, transformation and sink are one line apart; AI-15's minimal test is static reachability and nothing needs to be executed.
findings.impact: Whoever can steer a single line of the model's output runs arbitrary commands as the agent's process user. That process holds ANTHROPIC_API_KEY (answer.py:7) and sits in the deployment that carries the billing key (config/mcp.json:6), so the first command an attacker runs is the one that reads them. `shell=True` also means the shell metacharacters are live, so a benign-looking summary with a trailing `; curl ...` is enough — the payload does not have to look like a command.
findings.preconditions: Influence over the model's output, which the retrieval path of F-004 and F-005 supplies to any customer who files a ticket.
findings.recommendation: Delete the function. A support assistant has no operator-shell use case that justifies it, and the safe counterpart the file already contains (`summarize_and_render`, answer.py:51-56) shows the intended shape: validate the model's output against a closed set of operations and return data. If some operator tooling genuinely needs to run commands, the model may select an identifier from a fixed list of parameterised commands — never compose the string — and the execution must move into a process with no credentials, no network and an ephemeral filesystem.

triage.reason: No compensating control exists on this path: no sandbox declaration, container spec, seccomp profile, allowlist or schema validation appears anywhere in the target, and the call passes the raw string straight to a shell. The closed-list validation that would be this rule's artifact lives in a different function (answer.py:51-56) that this one does not call.

findings.limits: Establishes that model output reaches a shell sink in the code as written. No caller of `summarize_and_run` exists in the audited files, so how a deployment reaches it, and therefore its live blast radius, was not established — that bound is why severity is `high` rather than `critical`.

findings.title: Refund authorization decided by the model's text, with the authenticated subject discarded
findings.impact: A model that has read attacker text emits `{"tool": "refund", "account_id": <attacker>, "amount": <attacker>}` and the money moves. The same primitive reads any account through `lookup`, so it is a disclosure path across customers as well as a payment path. The permission rule this code needs — act only on the caller's own account, never refund — exists in the file at answer.py:36-43 and is simply not the function being audited here.
findings.preconditions: Influence over the model's decision output; for a support assistant that is ticket text, per F-004 and F-005.
findings.recommendation: Replace the body with `run_tool_scoped`'s discipline: take the object from `session["authenticated_account_id"]` and never from the model, and keep `refund` off the assistant's tool surface entirely, as that function already does by raising PermissionError. Authorize inside `issue_refund` and `lookup` against the concrete object rather than at the dispatcher, so no future caller can reintroduce the gap, and add a unit test that calls a sensitive tool with a session lacking permission and asserts it fails in authorization rather than in argument validation. Separately, put every irreversible effect behind a confirmation that renders the literal arguments (AI-07), not a summary the model wrote.

triage.reason: No unskippable layer authorizes this. `issue_refund` and `lookup` at answer.py:59-64 are the terminal implementations in scope and they perform the operation on the string they are handed; there is no middleware, no row-level policy and no end-user token forwarded to a backend that could authorize per object. The unused `session` parameter on line 27 is the positive evidence that identity was available at the decision point and was not applied.

findings.limits: Establishes that the dispatcher decides authorization from model-controlled text. The implementations of `issue_refund` and `lookup` in scope are stubs returning formatted strings, so the audit did not observe a real billing system being reached, nor whether one exists behind them that applies its own authorization.

findings.title: Retrieved documents interpolated into the prompt with no delimitation or provenance marking
findings.evidence:
agent/answer.py:11-13

    def build_prompt(question: str, docs: list[str]) -> str:
        joined = "\n".join(docs)
        return f"{SYSTEM}\n\nKnowledge:\n{joined}\n\nCustomer question: {question}"

`docs` is `list[str]` — the type itself has no room for an origin or a trust level — and the documents land in the same flat string as SYSTEM, separated only by the literal word `Knowledge:`, which a document can also contain. There is no delimiter the data cannot forge, no per-token marking of the data span, and no encoding of the block. The corpus these documents come from is written by `ingest_ticket` (memory.py:26-28) from customer ticket bodies.
findings.impact: Text written by a customer arrives in the model's context indistinguishable from the operator's instructions, which is the precondition for every downstream effect in this audit: it is what turns F-003's dispatcher into an attacker-controlled refund and F-002's shell into attacker-controlled command execution. The NCSC's 2025-12-08 framing applies directly — there is no parameterised-query equivalent here, so no phrasing added to SYSTEM repairs it.
findings.preconditions: The attacker can get a document into the retrieval corpus; filing a support ticket does it.
findings.recommendation: Use `build_prompt_marked` (answer.py:16-24), which the file already contains and which is the correct shape: one text block per document, wrapped with its `source` and `trust` attributes, in a user-role turn distinct from SYSTEM. Then delete `build_prompt` so the unsafe path cannot be selected. Add a test that indexes a document containing an instruction and an inert marker and asserts the marker never appears in the answer — spotlighting (arXiv:2403.14720) reports attack success dropping from over 50% to under 2% with this class of change. Pair it with F-005 so the `trust` attribute the marked builder renders is actually populated at ingestion.

triage.reason: There is no sanitizer, normalizer or delimiting layer between the retrieval store and this f-string; the target contains no filter of any kind on ingested text (the AI-20 sweep found no normalization code and no non-ASCII input handling). The delimited construction exists only as a separate function at answer.py:16 that this one does not call.

The value is attacker-controlled. `docs` is fed by the retrieval corpus, and memory.py:26-28 writes `ticket["body"]` — the free text of a customer support ticket — into that corpus with no review step, no closed-domain list and no approval gate. Tracing the value backwards ends at an external writer, not at a constant.

findings.inference: The link from the corpus that `ingest_ticket` writes to the `docs` parameter this function reads. No retrieval call — no `similarity_search`, retriever, or query — exists anywhere in the audited files, so that the indexed ticket bodies are the documents reaching `build_prompt` is inferred from the module structure and the shared `index` object, not observed in code.
findings.limits: Does not establish which builder a deployment calls, since neither has a caller in scope, and does not measure how much of a document survives into the context, since no retrieval or truncation logic is present.

findings.title: Customer tickets indexed into the retrieval corpus with no origin or trust metadata
findings.evidence:
agent/memory.py:26-28

    def ingest_ticket(ticket: dict, index) -> None:
        """Indexes a customer ticket into the retrieval store."""
        index.add_texts([ticket["body"]])

`add_texts` is called with the body alone. No `metadatas` argument, so the chunk enters the index carrying no origin, no trust level and no ticket identifier. The same file proves the API accepts all three: `ingest_ticket_marked` at memory.py:31-36 passes `metadatas=[{"origin": "customer-ticket", "trust": "untrusted", "ticket_id": ticket["id"]}]`.
findings.impact: The write path into the corpus is open to any customer, and once a chunk is in the index nothing records who contributed it. Three consequences follow from that single omission: retrieval cannot filter on trust, so there is no way to keep untrusted chunks out of a privileged answer; a poisoned document cannot be selectively reverted, only the whole index rebuilt; and no post-incident question about which ticket produced which answer can be answered. PoisonedRAG (USENIX Security 2025) sets the scale — five injected texts among 2.6 million documents forced the target answer 97% of the time — so the defence is provenance, not volume.
findings.preconditions: The attacker files a support ticket, which is the intended use of the channel.
findings.recommendation: Use `ingest_ticket_marked` (memory.py:31-36) and delete the unmarked function, so no chunk can enter the index without an origin, a trust level and a revert key. Then make the metadata load-bearing on the read side: require a trust filter in the retrieval call's signature so a caller cannot omit it, and feed the stored `origin`/`trust` into `build_prompt_marked`'s document attributes (F-004), which currently expects fields that the unmarked ingestion never writes.

triage.reason: Neither exculpation applies on this path. There is no origin or trust metadata for retrieval to filter on — that is the finding — and there is no human approval step or closed domain list: `ingest_ticket` takes a ticket dict and writes it to the index in one statement, with no queue, review flag or allowlist anywhere in the target.

findings.inference: That the indexed content reaches an answer. The retrieval read side is absent from the audited files — no `similarity_search`, `as_retriever` or query call exists — so the step from a poisoned chunk to a generated answer is argued from the module's stated purpose rather than observed.
findings.limits: Severity is held at `medium` deliberately: the boundary-crossing impact of untrusted text governing generation is already counted once, in F-004. What this finding adds on its own is that the corpus is unauditable and cannot be selectively reverted, which is real and bounded. The audit also did not see the index implementation, so whether the engine records provenance of its own accord could not be checked.

findings.title: Free-text model replies appended to a shared long-lived memory store
findings.evidence:
agent/memory.py:6 and 10-14

    STORE = Path("/var/lib/acme/agent-memory.json")
    ...
    def remember_from_reply(reply: str) -> None:
        """Persists whatever the model decided is worth keeping."""
        data = json.loads(STORE.read_text()) if STORE.exists() else {}
        data.setdefault("notes", []).append(reply)
        STORE.write_text(json.dumps(data))

The whole reply string is appended verbatim to `notes`. No schema, no key allowlist, no origin mark, no expiry and no size bound sit between the model's text and the file — the docstring states the design plainly. The destination is a single process-wide path with no subject in it, so `notes` is one list shared by every session that loads the store.
findings.impact: This is the persistence half of the injection problem. An instruction that survives into a reply — which, per F-004, may be text a customer wrote — is written to disk and re-enters later sessions carrying the authority of the assistant's own history, after the ticket that carried it is long gone. Because the store has no subject key, what one session writes is read back by every session, so a single successful injection becomes a durable, cross-user condition rather than a per-conversation one. MINJA (arXiv:2503.03704) reports over 95% injection success through queries alone with no access to the store, and SpAIware (2024-09) documented the consequence as continuous exfiltration across future sessions.
findings.preconditions: One reply containing attacker-influenced text, plus the store being read back on a later turn.
findings.recommendation: Delete `remember_from_reply` and route all persistence through `remember_preference` (memory.py:17-23), which is already the correct pattern: a closed key set, a typed value and a TTL. If a free-text note is genuinely required, it must be extracted into a typed field by a deterministic parser rather than copied, stored with its origin and trust level, expired, and made inspectable and deletable by the user. Key the store by authenticated subject either way, so one identity's memory cannot become another's.

triage.reason: Neither exculpation applies to this function. It stores free text derived from model output rather than fields from a closed schema — `ALLOWED_KEYS` at memory.py:7 exists but is enforced only in `remember_preference`, never here — and there is no expiry: the `ttl_days` field is written at memory.py:22 on the preference path only, while `notes` entries carry no expiry and no deletion path appears anywhere in the target.

findings.inference: That the persisted notes are read back into a later context. No reader of the `notes` array exists in the audited files, so the re-injection loop that produces the cross-session impact is argued from the module's declared role ('Long-lived assistant memory') and the persistence of the file, rather than observed in code.
findings.limits: Establishes the write path and the absence of any schema, mark or expiry on it. It does not establish which component calls the function or how the store is loaded into a prompt, and it does not assess per-user partitioning, which cannot be settled without the caller.

findings.title: Live-format billing credential written in plaintext into the MCP configuration
findings.impact: Everyone who can read the repository or the deployed configuration holds the billing API key, and any process that can read the file — including the agent itself through the shell of F-002 — can exfiltrate it. Because it is written into the environment of the `billing` MCP server, it is also the credential handed to the unpinned third-party package of F-008: a registry compromise there does not have to steal the key, it is given it at startup. GitGuardian (2026) found 24,008 unique secrets in MCP configuration files, 2,117 still valid, so this is the modal instance of a measured class rather than an unusual one.
findings.preconditions: Read access to the configuration file, which every developer, every CI job and every process on the host that runs the agent has.
findings.recommendation: Treat the value as compromised: rotate it at the provider first, then remove the literal. Replace it with `"${BILLING_API_KEY}"` to match line 11, and supply the value from a secret manager at process start. Confirm the key's absence from history at the source repository (`git log -p -- config/mcp.json`) — the audited copy is not a git repository, so prior versions could not be checked here — and scope the replacement key to the operations the assistant actually needs, with a spending limit.

triage.reason: Not a placeholder and not an obviously invalid example. It is a concrete 40-character value with a structured vendor prefix and a full 32-hex-character body, not `${VAR}`, `changeme` or a truncated sample. The `${DOCS_TOKEN}` form four lines below is the placeholder this file uses when it means one.

config/mcp.json is a runtime configuration consumed verbatim by the MCP client at startup; it is not compiled, minified or filtered by any build. The target contains no build script, packaging manifest, environment flag or test marker that would strip or override this entry, and the file is not under a test or fixture directory.

findings.limits: The key's validity was deliberately not tested — AI-11 directs escalation rather than verification against the provider — so the finding establishes that a credential-format literal is committed in configuration, not that this particular key currently authenticates. If the value turns out to be synthetic, the finding stands at the same location as the practice of writing literals where the file's own placeholder idiom exists, with the impact reduced accordingly.

findings.title: Third-party MCP server installed unpinned at every startup with a credential in its environment
findings.evidence:
config/mcp.json:3-7

    "command": "npx",
    "args": ["-y", "@acme/billing-mcp@latest"],
    "env": { "BILLING_API_KEY": "[REDACTED:secret]" }

The classification AI-09 asks for: third-party (a scoped registry package, not a path in this repository), unpinned (`@latest` resolves at every startup and `-y` suppresses the install prompt), no lockfile or integrity hash anywhere in the target, network-capable, and carrying a credential in its environment. That is the exact combination the procedure names as the finding. The `docs` entry at config/mcp.json:8-12 is the contrast: `node ./servers/docs/index.js`, a local path, with a placeholder token.
findings.impact: The code that runs is whatever was published under `@acme/billing-mcp` at the moment the agent last started, so the version reviewed and the version executed are not the same artifact by construction. Whoever gains control of that package name — a compromised maintainer account, a hijacked scope, a typosquat that the config is edited toward — executes on the host with the billing key already in the environment (F-007) and every other credential the process user holds. It is also the position from which tool poisoning and a rug pull operate: tool descriptions the client renders into the model's context can change between startups with nothing to compare them against.
findings.preconditions: Control of the published package under that name, or of the registry path to it. No access to the target's own systems is required.
findings.recommendation: Pin to an exact version with lockfile integrity, or run the server from a container image referenced by digest; drop `-y` so an unexpected install is visible. Record a hash per tool description at first approval and compare it at every startup, which converts a rug pull from an invisible change into a startup failure. Remove the credential from the server's environment per F-007 and scope the replacement to the minimum the billing tools need, so a supply-chain compromise does not inherit full billing authority. Vendor the server or move it first-party if the integration is long-lived.

triage.reason: No integrity layer sits in the path. The target contains no package-lock.json, no npm-shrinkwrap, no Dockerfile and no digest reference; `npx -y` with a floating tag resolves and executes directly with nothing to verify against. There is no allowlist or signature check the resolution must pass.

What executes is publisher-controlled, not fixed. `@latest` is a mutable pointer resolved at startup, so the artifact is chosen by whoever can publish under that name rather than by anything in this repository. The exculpating form — an exact version with lockfile integrity, or a local path such as the `docs` entry at line 10 — is absent here and present four lines below, which is what distinguishes the two entries.

findings.limits: This is supply-chain exposure, not an incident: nothing in this audit indicates the package is currently malicious, and it was deliberately not downloaded or executed. The server's own tool descriptions could not be inspected for the reason recorded in the AI-08 ruled_out entry.

findings.title: Dashboard serializer returns the whole customer record, including the national ID and internal-only fields
findings.evidence: app/serializers.py:18 -- `return asdict(customer)` over a dataclass that declares `national_id`, `internal_risk_score` and `support_notes` alongside `id`, `email` and `full_name` (lines 8-13). The same module declares the intended public projection three lines later: `PUBLIC_FIELDS = ("id", "email", "full_name")` (line 21). A response therefore carries `national_id`: [REDACTED:pii] and free-text `support_notes`: [REDACTED:pii] on top of the declared public set. Module docstring, line 1: "API serializers for the customer-facing dashboard."
findings.impact: Over-exposure of data with a technical cause (a privacy risk, not a broken access control -- no cross-customer read was demonstrated and none is claimed). Three fields beyond the module's own declared public set leave the process on every serialized response: a direct identifier the dashboard does not display (`national_id`), an internal assessment about the person (`internal_risk_score`) and a free-text field that PRV-01 warns can hold more personal data than any field named `email` (`support_notes`). Once the object has left the server, not rendering those fields in the interface protects nothing: they are in the response body, in the browser cache and in any intermediary that stores it.
findings.preconditions: A request handler serializes with `customer_response()` rather than with `customer_response_public()`.
findings.recommendation: Make the projection the only way out rather than one of two options: remove `customer_response()`, or reduce it to a private helper that `customer_response_public()` filters, so no caller can reach `asdict()` directly. Pin the public shape with a test that fails when a field is added to the dataclass and not declared in `PUBLIC_FIELDS` -- the docstring on line 25 already claims such a test exists and no test file is present in the target.
findings.inference: Reachability. No route, view or caller exists anywhere in the target, so that the customer-facing dashboard calls `customer_response()` rather than its allowlisted sibling is read from the module and function docstrings, not observed.

triage.reason: `customer_response_public()` (app/serializers.py:24-26) is a sibling function, not a layer that cannot be skipped: the target contains no base serializer, no response middleware and no outbound schema between `asdict()` and the caller. A control that a caller has to choose -- and may forget -- is explicitly not this rule.

A boundary is crossed and the code names it: the module docstring declares these serializers are for the customer-facing dashboard, so the second principal is the browser. `internal_risk_score` and `support_notes` are internal-audience content about the person, produced on one side of that boundary and delivered to the other.

findings.limits: Establishes what the function returns, not which endpoint returns it and not whether a caller can obtain another customer's record: no query, authorization or tenancy layer is in scope, so PRV-05 was not reached from here.

findings.title: Request logging writes the caller's email address and national ID into the log record
findings.evidence: app/logging_setup.py:11-12 -- `logger.info("request path=%s user=%s email=%s national_id=%s", path, user["id"], user["email"], user["national_id"])`, so each record carries email=[REDACTED:pii] and national_id=[REDACTED:pii]. `RedactingFormatter` is declared at line 20 and never installed: `grep -rn "setFormatter|basicConfig|dictConfig|addHandler|getLogger"` over the whole target returns no match, and `logger` is a parameter the caller supplies.
findings.impact: Personal data is copied into the log store, which carries none of the database's controls: different retention, usually no encryption at rest, and far broader read access (engineering plus whichever aggregator receives the stream). `national_id` is a direct identifier, so a log line is enough to re-identify without any join. Two routes reach the sink even where the formatter is attached: a handler configured without it, and any structured, JSON or APM handler that serializes `record.args` rather than the rendered string -- the redaction at line 25 rewrites the formatted text only, after the values are already on the record.
findings.preconditions: A caller uses `log_request()` rather than `log_request_redacted()`, and the logger it passes has at least one handler that does not apply `RedactingFormatter` or that consumes the record's arguments.
findings.recommendation: Remove `log_request()` or make it delegate to `log_request_redacted()`, so the opaque identifier is the only thing a caller can log. If the redaction is to stay as defence in depth, apply it on the record -- a `logging.Filter` over `args` and `extra` -- rather than on the rendered string, install it in the logging configuration that actually ships, and add the test PRV-09's exculpation requires: emit each field name through the configured logger and assert the value does not appear in the output.
findings.inference: Whether the deployed logging configuration attaches `RedactingFormatter` to every handler that receives these records. The call and the interpolated fields are observed in the code; the rendering at the sink is not, because no logging configuration exists in the target.

triage.reason: The redaction is not in a layer that cannot be skipped. `RedactingFormatter` (app/logging_setup.py:20-25) is per-handler, has no installation site anywhere in the target, and operates on the already-formatted string, so a handler without it or one that serializes `record.args` reaches the sink around it. PRV-09's exculpation additionally requires a test covering the field list, and the target contains none. The regex itself covers three field names in `key=value` form only, which is a narrower guarantee than the record holds.

The two values are direct identifiers of a natural person: `email` and `national_id` as declared on the Customer dataclass (app/serializers.py:9 and 11). PRV-01 decides that classification from the schema, and here the schema states it.

findings.limits: Does not establish where these logs land, who can read them, how long they are kept or whether they leave the organization: no aggregator, retention or APM configuration is in scope. No log output was produced -- nothing was executed.

findings.title: Full name, email and national ID are interpolated into the prompt sent to the external model provider
findings.evidence: app/assistant.py:12-13 builds `f"Customer {customer['full_name']} ({customer['email']}, id {customer['national_id']}) had these events: {events}. ..."` -- carrying [REDACTED:pii] in three interpolations -- and lines 15-18 pass it straight to `client.messages.create(...)` on the external client constructed at line 6. The whole `events` list is stringified as-is, including each event's free-text `note`, which the pseudonymous variant at line 25 explicitly strips.
findings.impact: Privacy risk arising from a designed transfer, not a broken control: on every summary, a direct identifier set (name, email address, national ID) plus the full event history including free text leaves the organization for a third-party processor. What happens next -- request logging, retention window, use for training -- is provider-side configuration that is not in this repository. If those requests are retained, the exposure is durable and not selectively deletable, which is the variant PRV-07 warns about; that is what would raise this above medium.
findings.preconditions: A caller uses `summarize_account()` rather than `summarize_account_pseudonymous()`.
findings.recommendation: Route every summary through the pseudonymous builder and delete the identifying one, keeping the token map inside the system so re-identification stays local. Strip free-text event fields on the way out rather than relying on the caller. Record the criterion for what a prompt may carry, not only today's field list, since a field that is necessary now stops being so after a product change. Separately, obtain and file the provider-side retention and training settings as an engagement artifact -- that is the only thing that can turn the FP-08 answer below into something other than UNKNOWN.
findings.inference: Two links are argued rather than observed: no caller in the target selects between the two prompt builders, and the provider-side retention configuration lives outside the repository, so what becomes of the prompt after transmission cannot be read here.

triage.reason: `summarize_account_pseudonymous()` (app/assistant.py:21-31) is an alternative function, not an enforced layer: nothing routes prompt construction through it, and no scrubbing step sits between the f-string at line 12 and the `client.messages.create` call at line 15.

The boundary is organizational and named in the code: the payload leaves for an external provider through the client constructed at app/assistant.py:4 and 6. The provider is a second principal by construction.

The exculpation PRV-07 accepts -- a zero-retention or no-training arrangement verifiable in the provider configuration -- lives outside this repository, and no exported console setting, contract, ticket or written statement was provided with the target. Absence of that evidence is UNKNOWN and never HOLDS, and it is what caps this finding at probable.

findings.limits: Establishes only what leaves the process. It says nothing about what the provider does with the payload, and the provider console was not consulted -- that would require credentials and an authorization this engagement does not carry.

findings.title: Account deletion marks only the customers table, so the purge job clears one store while appearing to clear five
findings.evidence: jobs/lifecycle.py:10 -- `UPDATE customers SET deleted_at = now() WHERE id = %s` is the only statement in the target that ever writes `deleted_at`, and it writes it in one table. jobs/lifecycle.py:15-17 then loops over `STORES = ("customers", "events", "exports", "search_index", "backups")` (line 5) issuing `DELETE FROM <store> WHERE deleted_at IS NOT NULL AND deleted_at < %s`. For the four stores other than `customers`, no path in the target ever satisfies `deleted_at IS NOT NULL`, so those four deletes match nothing.
findings.impact: Privacy risk in retention: after a deletion request the person's data survives indefinitely in the event stream, the exports, the search index and the backups, while the account row disappears after the 30-day window. The shape of the code is what makes it durable -- `purge_expired()` iterates every store and reads as full coverage, so a reviewer confirming that deletion propagates finds exactly the loop they were looking for. A later data-subject request would also be answered from `customers` alone while four other stores still hold the record.
findings.preconditions: No writer outside the target sets `deleted_at` on `events`, `exports`, `search_index` or `backups`.
findings.recommendation: Do not leave propagation implicit in a column nothing sets. Either have `delete_account()` mark every store in `STORES` in one transaction, or drive `purge_expired()` from the customer's `deleted_at` by key or join instead of from a per-store column. Handle the two stores that are not rows on their own terms: a search index needs a delete-by-document call and a backup set needs a rotation policy, neither of which a `DELETE` reaches. Prove it with the PRV-04 minimal test -- a synthetic account written into all five stores, then a count in each after the cutoff.
findings.inference: That no other writer sets `deleted_at` on the four derived stores. `delete_account()` is the only one inside the target, but the schema (DDL, triggers, defaults) and any other service that writes those tables are outside it.

triage.reason: A mandatory database-side layer -- `ON DELETE CASCADE` from `customers`, a trigger, a row-level policy -- would cover part of this, and no DDL is present in the target to check. Worth recording the shape such a control would have to take: `delete_account()` issues an UPDATE, so no referential cascade fires there at all; only the DELETE inside `purge_expired()` could cascade, and a cascade cannot reach a search index or a backup set. It could not be established from the artifact, so UNKNOWN, which caps this finding at probable.

The retention half -- bucket lifecycle rules, backup rotation, index reindexing -- lives in infrastructure outside this repository, and no exported configuration, policy document or written retention statement accompanied the target. Under FP-08 that is UNKNOWN, not HOLDS.

findings.limits: Does not establish the real retention of the backups or of the search index, nor whether an out-of-band process purges them. No database was touched and no row was counted; the conclusion is read from the two statements and the store list.

findings.title: Third-party analytics and advertising tags are emitted unconditionally, bypassing the consent gate that exists beside them
findings.evidence: jobs/lifecycle.py:20-25 -- `load_trackers(page)` takes no consent argument and returns two third-party script tags with no condition: `cdn.metrics.example/collect.js` carrying a site identifier, and `ads.partner.example/px.js`. The consent-aware sibling at lines 28-32 takes a `consent` dict, returns `[]` when `consent["analytics"]` is falsy, and returns the metrics tag only -- the advertising pixel appears in no accepted category anywhere in the target.
findings.impact: Two readings, and they should be reported separately. As a privacy risk: on any page rendering this list, the visitor's IP address, user agent, page path and whatever cookie each vendor sets reach an analytics vendor and an advertising vendor on first render, before any interaction and irrespective of what a consent manager recorded -- the pattern PRV-06 describes as the SDK that loads anyway and only flips a flag. As a product decision: the advertising pixel is absent from the consent-aware variant, so shipping it at all is a choice about which third parties the product feeds, and it belongs to the product owner with the cost of keeping it and the cost of dropping it stated, not to engineering as a defect.
findings.preconditions: A page template renders the list returned by `load_trackers()`.
findings.recommendation: Make the consent-aware function the only producer of tag markup and delete `load_trackers()`, so no template can reach the ungated list. Decide explicitly whether the advertising pixel belongs to any category rather than letting it inherit the analytics one, and give it its own if it is kept. Keep the list PRV-06 says nobody holds: which tag is emitted under which category, and what each vendor receives -- and confirm it against observed traffic, since the presence of a tag says nothing about what it sends.
findings.inference: Reachability. Neither function has a caller and no template exists in the target, so which of the two a page renders is read from their names and docstrings rather than observed.

triage.reason: The consent check lives inside the alternative function (jobs/lifecycle.py:30) rather than in a layer on the way out. Nothing stops a template calling `load_trackers()` directly, and the target contains no tag manager, no CSP and no rendering middleware that could enforce the gate for both paths.

Two second principals are named in the code by their own domains: `cdn.metrics.example` and `ads.partner.example` (jobs/lifecycle.py:23-24). This is not first-party telemetry staying on project infrastructure; the data leaves for third parties.

findings.limits: Establishes what the function returns, not what those vendors collect -- only observed traffic would show that, and no request was made and no page was loaded. The consent manager itself is not in scope, so whether a recorded refusal is honoured anywhere else could not be checked.
